title: Trump pardons former Maricopa County sheriff Joe Arpaio
description_medium: Trump pardoned Joe Arpaio on August 25, 2017, after a federal judge found the former Maricopa County sheriff guilty of criminal contempt for disobeying a court order in an immigration-enforcement case. The pardon came before sentencing and ended the prosecution, though the court declined to erase the conviction. The White House cited Arpaio’s decades in law enforcement.
description_long:
Joe Arpaio, Maricopa County’s sheriff for 24 years, was convicted of criminal contempt after disobeying a federal court order tied to his office’s immigration patrols. The underlying order required changes to practices that a judge found had unlawfully targeted Latino drivers. Arpaio was found guilty on July 31, 2017; his sentencing had not yet occurred when Trump granted him a pardon on August 25.

The pardon ended the prosecution before a sentence was imposed. Arpaio later asked the court to vacate the conviction; the district court dismissed the prosecution but declined to erase its finding of guilt, and the Ninth Circuit reviewed that dispute. The White House defended the grant by emphasizing Arpaio’s military, police, and DEA service and his record as sheriff. The clemency thus relieved Arpaio from punishment for the contempt conviction while leaving the court’s determination intact, a distinction later made central to the legal proceedings.
source_access_notes: White House statement read for grant date and its account of Arpaio’s service; Ninth Circuit opinion read for conviction, pardon timing, and post-pardon disposition; DOJ clemency list consulted for the offense; contemporaneous Guardian report read for the underlying immigration-order context.
rationale: The Ninth Circuit opinion establishes that the pardon preceded sentencing, the prosecution ended, and the conviction remained; the White House states its rationale. The contempt finding followed disobedience of an order in the immigration-enforcement case.

title: Trump pardons Army Major Mathew Golsteyn before murder trial
description_medium: On November 15, 2019, Trump fully pardoned Army Major Mathew Golsteyn, who was awaiting trial for allegedly killing a suspected Taliban bombmaker in Afghanistan. Golsteyn said he shot the man after concluding he remained a threat. The White House cited the long investigation and support from lawmakers and veterans; Golsteyn had not been tried or convicted.
description_long:
Mathew Golsteyn, an Army major and West Point graduate, faced a military murder trial over the 2010 killing of an Afghan detainee whom an informant had identified as a Taliban bombmaker. Two Marines had been killed by an improvised explosive device in the same broader operation. The White House said the Army released the detainee because of shortcomings in the Afghan detention system; Golsteyn later said he shot him because he believed he would continue to endanger U.S. forces and Afghan partners. The alleged killing had not gone to trial.

Trump signed a full pardon for Golsteyn on November 15, 2019, alongside a pardon for Army Lieutenant Clint Lorance and an order restoring Navy SEAL Edward Gallagher’s rank. The administration described the decade-long inquiry and broad support from lawmakers and military figures as reasons for clemency. The DOJ records the underlying murder charge as charged but not tried or convicted. The grant therefore stopped a pending military prosecution without a court-martial verdict, and the differing descriptions of the shooting remained unresolved in court.
source_access_notes: White House November 15, 2019 statement read for the alleged killing and stated rationale; Washington Post report read for the military justice context; DOJ clemency list read for the charged, untried offense.
rationale: The White House and DOJ distinguish the charged allegation from a conviction and identify the pardon as pretrial; the administration’s account of the killing and its stated clemency rationale are attributed.

title: Trump pardons former congressman Duncan Hunter after campaign-funds conviction
description_medium: Trump fully pardoned former California congressman Duncan Hunter on December 22, 2020. Hunter had pleaded guilty to conspiring to convert campaign funds to personal use and received an 11-month prison sentence scheduled to begin in January. Prosecutors said he and his wife used more than $250,000 for personal expenses. The White House cited congressional supporters and an argument that the conduct could have been handled by the FEC.
description_long:
Duncan Hunter represented California’s 50th congressional district from 2013 to 2020 and served as a Marine officer before entering Congress. In December 2019, he pleaded guilty to conspiring with his wife and campaign manager, Margaret Hunter, to convert campaign funds for personal expenses. Federal prosecutors said the couple spent more than $250,000 on private costs over several years. The court sentenced Hunter to 11 months in prison, scheduled to begin in January 2021.

Trump granted him a full pardon on December 22, 2020, before he began serving that term. The White House cited requests from members of Congress and former FEC commissioner Bradley Smith’s view that the conduct could have been treated as a civil campaign-finance matter. The plea, conviction, and sentence remained part of the official case record; the pardon relieved Hunter of federal punishment. The following day, Trump also pardoned Margaret Hunter for her role in the same campaign-funds conspiracy, a timing that made the two actions part of one clemency episode.
source_access_notes: White House clemency statement read for grant date and stated rationale; DOJ plea and sentencing releases read for the guilty plea, amounts, and sentence; DOJ pardon list consulted for the official entry.
rationale: The DOJ plea and sentencing releases establish the campaign-funds conspiracy and 11-month term; the White House reports the clemency date and its civil-enforcement argument. The pardon came before the scheduled prison term.

title: Trump pardons Blackwater guard Nicholas Slatten for Nisour Square killings
description_medium: Trump pardoned Nicholas Slatten on December 22, 2020, while he was serving life for murder in the 2007 Nisour Square shooting in Baghdad. Slatten and three other Blackwater contractors were convicted over civilians killed during a convoy shooting. Their defenders disputed the convictions, while critics said clemency diminished accountability for Iraqi victims; UN experts called the pardons an affront to justice.
description_long:
Nicholas Slatten, a former Blackwater security contractor, was convicted of first-degree murder for the killing of an Iraqi civilian during the 2007 Nisour Square shooting in Baghdad. Prosecutors said the convoy opened fire on civilians at a crowded intersection. Slatten’s first conviction was overturned on appeal, but he was retried and again received a life sentence; three other contractors were convicted of manslaughter and related offenses.

Trump granted Slatten a full pardon on December 22, 2020, together with pardons for Paul Slough, Evan Liberty, and Dustin Heard. The White House cited the men’s military service and raised concerns about evidence in Slatten’s trial. The grants drew sharp criticism: UN human-rights experts said pardoning the contractors was an affront to justice and the victims, while defense lawyers welcomed the decision. The clemency ended the federal punishment for Slatten’s conviction, but the dispute over the shooting and the effect of the pardons on accountability for civilian deaths continued well beyond the grant.
source_access_notes: DOJ sentencing release read for Slatten’s murder conviction; CBS/AP report read for the shooting, group convictions, appeals, and public reaction; UN experts’ statement read for the criticism; White House statement and DOJ clemency table read for the pardon and its stated basis.
rationale: DOJ records Slatten’s murder conviction and life term; contemporaneous coverage supplies the appellate chronology and responses to the grant. The White House’s stated concerns and the UN experts’ condemnation capture the dispute surrounding the pardon.

title: Trump pardons Margaret Hunter after campaign-funds conspiracy conviction
description_medium: Trump granted Margaret Hunter a full pardon on December 23, 2020, one day after pardoning her husband, former congressman Duncan Hunter. She had pleaded guilty to conspiring to use campaign money for personal expenses and was sentenced to three years’ probation, including eight months of home detention. The White House said a former FEC commissioner viewed the conduct as a civil matter.
description_long:
Margaret Hunter managed her husband Duncan Hunter’s congressional campaign and pleaded guilty in June 2019 to conspiring with him to convert campaign funds to personal use. Federal prosecutors said the couple diverted more than $200,000 for personal expenses and used campaign accounts for dozens of transactions. Her plea included cooperation with the government’s case against her husband. In August 2020, she was sentenced to three years’ probation, including eight months of home detention.

Trump granted her a full pardon on December 23, 2020, the day after he pardoned Duncan Hunter. The White House cited former FEC commissioner Bradley Smith’s view that the conduct underlying her plea should have been addressed as a civil matter. The pardon resolved the federal punishment for her conviction; it did not alter her guilty plea or the public record of the campaign-finance case. The one-day sequence and the White House’s explicit connection to the former congressman’s pardon make clear the two grants addressed the same underlying campaign-funds conduct.
source_access_notes: White House December 23 statement read for the pardon date, stated FEC rationale and connection to Duncan Hunter; DOJ plea and sentencing releases read for the amount, cooperation and sentence; DOJ clemency table consulted for the case record.
rationale: DOJ releases document the campaign-funds conspiracy, plea cooperation and sentence; the White House explicitly links Margaret’s pardon to the prior pardon of her husband for the same conduct.
